content_voiceover: This slide is a high yield classification of immune mediated hemolytic anemia by antibody thermal activity. Cold-active antibodies, active around zero to five degrees Celsius, cause cold agglutinin disease, which can be primary or secondary to lymphoproliferative disorders like Waldenstrom's, CLL, or infections — classically Mycoplasma pneumonia and infectious mononucleosis. Also in this category is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, caused by the Donath-Landsteiner biphasic hemolysin, historically linked to syphilis and now more often to viral infections in children. Warm-active antibodies, active at body temperature, cause warm AIHA, which is idiopathic in about half of cases or secondary to lymphoproliferative disease, autoimmune disorders like lupus, viral infections, or immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy — a modern and increasingly tested association. Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia has several mechanisms worth memorizing: the drug absorption type with penicillin, neoantigen formation with quinidine, true autoimmune induction with alpha-methyldopa, and non-immune protein adsorption with first generation cephalosporins. Finally, transplant-associated hemolytic anemia occurs with ABO-mismatched stem cell or solid organ transplants, including the passenger lymphocyte syndrome.
keypoints: Cold Ab (0-5°C): CAD (Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma), PCH (Donath-Landsteiner)
Warm Ab (37°C): idiopathic/secondary AIHA (SLE, lymphoma, checkpoint inhibitors)
Transplant-associated HA: ABO mismatch, passenger lymphocyte syndrome
keypoint_voiceover: Split immune hemolytic anemia by antibody temperature. Cold agglutinin disease and paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria are classically linked to Mycoplasma, mononucleosis, and the Donath-Landsteiner antibody. Warm AIHA is idiopathic or secondary to lupus, lymphoma, or checkpoint inhibitors. For drug-induced hemolysis, memorize the four mechanisms — penicillin absorption, quinidine neoantigen, methyldopa true autoimmune, and cephalosporin non-immune adsorption.
